Results Preview

Published

June 17, 2026

Note

Unless specified otherwise, temperature refers to the 7 day mean of temperature

Main Effects

Temperature Effects

Here, we estimate the impact of temperature on mental health directly, without the influence of shocks.

In particular, we estimate

\[ Y_{ict} = + \beta_1 Temp_{ict} + X_{ict}'\Gamma + \alpha_c + \lambda_m + \delta_y + \pi_w + \varepsilon_{ict}, \]

where \(Y_{ict}\) is respondent \(i\)’s CES-D z-score (or sleep hours) in community \(c\) at interview date \(t\), \(Temp_{ict}\) is the temperature measure shown in the tab, and the remaining terms are demographic and fixed effects described in the main effects section

Non-linear Effects of Temperature

Following Fritz, 2026 I estimate the non-linear impacts of temperature on mental health. The effect of wetbulb is very linear with hotter days being better for mental health. For regular temperature, there is no clear pattern (most coeffs are close to null) with one coeff, days between 21-22.5 being an improvment over our reference temperature

Main Table

The main shock tables estimate heat amplification among baseline stressor groups. Let \(Y_{ict}\) be respondent \(i\)’s CES-D z-score in community \(c\) at interview date \(t\), \(H_{ict}\) be the temperature measure shown in the tab, \(X_{ict}\) be age, female, years of education, married, and widowed controls, and \(\alpha_c\), \(\lambda_m\), \(\delta_y\), and \(\pi_w\) be community, month, year, and wave fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered by kecamatan in the paper tables.

For the baseline job-loss shock:

\[ Y_{ict} = \beta_1 H_{ict} + \beta_2 J_{ict} + \beta_3 (H_{ict} \times J_{ict}) + X_{ict}'\Gamma + \alpha_c + \lambda_m + \delta_y + \pi_w + \varepsilon_{ict}, \]

where \(J_{ict}\) indicates job loss within the past six months while currently not working. The reported shock coefficient is \(\beta_3\).

For baseline-group shocks observed before the later exposure period:

\[ Y_{ict} = \beta_1 H_{ict} + \beta_2 G_i + \beta_3 P_t + \beta_4 (G_i \times P_t) + \beta_5 (H_{ict} \times G_i) + \beta_6 (H_{ict} \times P_t) + \beta_7 (H_{ict} \times G_i \times P_t) + X_{ict}'\Gamma + \alpha_c + \lambda_m + \delta_y + \varepsilon_{ict}. \]

Here \(G_i\) is the baseline group indicator and \(P_t\) is the post indicator. The palm and coal columns use \(P_t=\mathbf{1}\{\text{IFLS5}\}\); the fuel column is estimated within IFLS5 and uses \(P_t=\mathbf{1}\{\text{interview date} \ge \text{2014-11-18}\}\). The reported shock coefficient is \(\beta_7\).

Robustness

Palm Farmer

Group Transitions

We mark anyone who was a farmer in a palm region in the IFLS as a palm farmer. We use their status in Wave 4. The table below plots the number of switchers (i.e. those who stopped being palm farmers due to moving or not being farmers anymore or those who are palm farmers in wave 5 but not 4).

Group Respondents Share of IFLS4 palm farmers
IFLS4 palm farmers in IFLS5 sample 2,681 100.0%
Still palm farmers in IFLS5 2,035 75.9%
No longer palm farmers in IFLS5 646 24.1%
New IFLS5 palm farmers 1,858

Alternate Specs

  • Palm farmer: Main Spec for comparison
  • Palm farmer in both waves: restricts the group to people who are palm farmers in both wave 4 and wave 5
  • Palm farmer in wave 5: restricts the group to people who are palm farmers in wave 5, regardless of wave 4 status
  • Farmer in non-palm region: tests whether farming alone, outside palm regions, drives the result.
  • Farmer in palm-region with main crop that isn’t palm: restricts palm-region farmers to households reporting a named, non-other IFLS4 main crop.
  • Non-farmer in palm region: tests whether living in palm regions alone drives the result.
  • IFLS4 palm x price gap: replaces the binary palm group with the standardized IFLS4-to-IFLS5 palm price gap for IFLS4 palm farmers.
  • Palm farmer, kec x post FE: repeats the headline palm specification with kecamatan-by-IFLS5 fixed effects.

Fuel Cut Placebo Dates

The fuel shock specification uses the removal of the fuel subsidies as a shock. To test that this was indeed a shock whose interaction with mental health is causing impact, the figures report the main coefficient on the variable of interest, \((H_{ict} \times G_i \times P_t)\), where \(P_t\) is arbitrarily chosen date (the true fuel subsidy cut date is November 18, 2014 and highlighted in the figure).

Glossary

Outcomes

CES-D z-score (cesd_z): standardized depressive-symptom score from the IFLS CES-D items. The raw CES-D score is standardized within survey wave, so coefficients are in wave-specific standard-deviation units.

CES-D raw score (cesd_raw): unstandardized depressive-symptom score. Higher values indicate more depressive symptoms.

Temperature Measures

All main temperature variables are attached to the respondent’s interview date and geography. Variables ending in _dev are centered deviations from the mean of that measure in the analysis file. Thus a one-unit change in a temperature deviation is one degree Celsius for temperature levels, or one day for hot-day counts.

Daily mean temperature (tmean_c_dev): mean air temperature on the interview date, in degrees Celsius, minus the analysis-sample mean of daily mean temperature.

7-day mean temperature (tmean_7d_dev): rolling 7-day mean of daily mean temperature ending on the interview date, with at least four observed days, minus the analysis-sample mean of that rolling measure.

30-day mean temperature (tmean_30d_dev): rolling 30-day mean of daily mean temperature ending on the interview date, with at least 15 observed days, minus the analysis-sample mean of that rolling measure.

Daily maximum temperature (tmax_c_dev): maximum air temperature on the interview date, in degrees Celsius, minus the analysis-sample mean of daily maximum temperature.

Daily minimum temperature (tmin_c_dev): minimum air temperature on the interview date, in degrees Celsius, minus the analysis-sample mean of daily minimum temperature.

7-day minimum temperature (tmin_7d_dev): rolling 7-day mean of daily minimum temperature ending on the interview date, with at least four observed days, minus the analysis-sample mean of that rolling measure.

Wet-bulb temperature (wetbulb_c_dev): interview-date daily mean wet-bulb temperature, in degrees Celsius, minus the analysis-sample mean. Wet-bulb temperature is computed from hourly air temperature and dewpoint using relative humidity and the Stull wet-bulb approximation, then averaged to the local day.

7-day wet-bulb temperature (wetbulb_7d_dev): rolling 7-day mean of daily wet-bulb temperature ending on the interview date, with at least four observed days, minus the analysis-sample mean of that rolling measure.

30-day wet-bulb temperature (wetbulb_30d_dev): rolling 30-day mean of daily wet-bulb temperature ending on the interview date, with at least 15 observed days, minus the analysis-sample mean of that rolling measure.

Survey-hour wet-bulb temperature (wetbulb_hr_dev): wet-bulb temperature at the respondent’s interview hour, in degrees Celsius, minus the analysis-sample mean of survey-hour wet-bulb temperature.

7-day hot days (hot30_7d_dev): count of days in the rolling 7-day window ending on the interview date for which daily maximum temperature exceeds \(30^\circ\)C, minus the analysis-sample mean of that count.

Heat (heat_c_dev): alias for daily mean temperature deviation in the final analysis tables.

Shock And Group Status

Palm-farmer household (palm_farmer_hh_ifls4): baseline IFLS4 household indicator equal to one if any household member worked in agriculture and lived in a province classified as a palm-producing province. This is a region-by-sector proxy for palm exposure, not direct observation that the household produced oil palm.

Palm shock: the main preview shock specification uses palm_farmer_hh_ifls4 x ifls5 x heat. It compares heat sensitivity for baseline palm-proxy households after the palm-price decline period relative to other households and the earlier wave.

Coal-worker household (coal_worker_hh_ifls4): baseline IFLS4 household indicator equal to one if any household member worked in mining and lived in a province classified as a coal-producing province. This is a region-by-sector proxy for coal exposure.

Coal shock: the main preview shock specification uses coal_worker_hh_ifls4 x ifls5 x heat. It compares heat sensitivity for baseline coal-proxy households in IFLS5 relative to other households and the earlier wave.

Urban vehicle-owning household (urban_vehicle_hh_ifls4): baseline IFLS4 household indicator equal to one if the household was urban and reported vehicle ownership. This group is used as the fuel-subsidy-cut exposure group.

Post-subsidy-cut interview (post_subsidy): indicator equal to one for interviews on or after November 18, 2014, the fuel-subsidy-cut date used in the pipeline.

Fuel shock: the main preview shock specification uses urban_vehicle_hh_ifls4 x post_subsidy x heat within IFLS5. It compares heat sensitivity for baseline urban vehicle-owning households interviewed after the subsidy cut relative to comparable IFLS5 interviews before the cut.

Job loss within 6 months (job_loss_180d): indicator equal to one when the respondent reports a last job loss within 180 days of the interview and is not currently working. The job-loss columns interact this contemporaneous stressor with heat.

Fixed Effects And Controls

Community fixed effects: fixed effects for the respondent’s kecamatan-level location. These absorb time-invariant community differences.

Kecamatan: Indonesian subdistrict. In this preview, kecamatan is the community-level geography used for fixed effects and clustered standard errors.

Kabupaten: Indonesian district or regency, the administrative unit above kecamatan and below province.

Month and year fixed effects: fixed effects for interview month-of-year and calendar year. The headline identifying variation is daily weather variation around interview timing within communities, months, and years.

Wave fixed effects: IFLS4/IFLS5 survey-wave fixed effects used in pooled specifications when the sample includes both waves.

Controls: age, female, years of education, married, and widowed.
